metadata.one_insight: An agent fails when it takes a real action and no one catches it — so the engineering job is a system that catches it, not a smarter model.

beats.narration_text: This video was made by Mubin Modi. This is a video about how agentic systems work, explained with an example. You've used a chatbot that rescheduled something for you, and it worked. Nobody asks the other question: what happens when it doesn't? A chatbot that's wrong hands you bad text. An agent that's wrong cancels your appointment. Let's open up what actually sits behind that green checkmark.

Four layers stand between the two.

beats.narration_text: An agent fails because the model acted — and no one checked. So the fix is oversight, not a better model. Everything that follows is that oversight, built one layer at a time.

beats.narration_text: Here's the frame for everything else. Changing a calendar entry is reversible enough to automate — carefully. So the agent proposes. Code checks the slot is real and the appointment is yours. You approve, explicitly. Only then does the tool run. Four layers, four different failure modes caught. The agent is never the final word on its own action.

beats.upgrade_note: LayerStack pins its caption at bottom:96 and stacks cards from `top` at 130px pitch. With the default top=150 the fourth card collides with the caption (caught in QC); top=100 clears it. Any future beat using four LayerStack layers needs the same override.

beats.narration_text: Watch one sentence go through it. Move my Tuesday appointment to Thursday afternoon. Classify the intent — reschedule, not cancel. Resolve which appointment. Check whether Thursday is open. Get a yes. Then write. Broken into ordered steps, each one is testable on its own. Left whole, it's a single guess you can only grade at the end.

beats.narration_text: Layer two can only check what it can see. So the agent never hands the backend the raw sentence — it hands it these fields. Which appointment, what new time, why, whether confirmation is required. Free text arriving at a system is unvalidatable, and it's an injection surface. Narrow typed parameters are what turn a tool call into something code can check before it runs.
beats.new_visual_element: The tool contract — what the backend actually receives

beats.narration_text: Now the failure that survives all of that. Every step returns clean. The final message reads: your appointment is confirmed for Thursday. No exception thrown. And it's still wrong — step five never checked the twenty-four-hour rescheduling policy. Grade the last sentence and this passes. Grade the whole trace, step by step, and it doesn't. That's the difference between a demo and production.

beats.narration_text: So: rescheduling one appointment touched almost all of it. Four layers between the agent and the calendar. One sentence broken into ordered, testable steps. Typed fields instead of free text, so code has something to check. And a grader that reads the whole trace, because a clean final message can still hide a skipped rule. None of this exists because the model is bad. It exists because acting in the real world means being wrong safely.

props.artifactHeading: What actually stands behind the checkmark
artifactLines: The agent proposes, code validates, the human approves, and only then does the tool run — four layers, four different failure modes caught.
One sentence becomes ordered, testable steps; left whole it is a single guess you can only grade at the end.
Typed fields, never free text — that is what makes a tool call checkable before it runs, and one less injection surface.
Grade the whole trace, not the final sentence: a perfect message can still hide a rule that was never evaluated.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — read this one with me. “Take one action your agent can take on a real system. Write the four layers for it: what the agent proposes, what code can validate before it runs, what the human must explicitly approve, and what the tool actually executes. Then name one failure that gets through all four.” That last clause is the exercise — the first four are easy to fill in; the fifth is where you find out whether your layers are real. Check the answer three ways: is layer two a check code could actually run, is the approval explicit rather than inferred, and would your logs catch the failure it names?
